paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial myopathy with lactic acidosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the PNPLA8 gene. Saunders et al. (2015) described a girl with a progressive mitochondrial myopathy, neurologic decline and lactic acidosis, whose muscle showed degenerating mitochondria. Later reports widened the phenotype. Abdel-Hamid et al. (2024) recognized congenital, infantile, childhood and adult-onset forms. Nakamura et al. (2024) concluded that PNPLA8-related neurologic disease is a continuum, ranging from developmental and/or degenerative epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy to childhood-onset neurodegeneration.

paragraphs.text: Mastaglia et al. (1980) described a 23-year-old man with a mitochondrial myopathy. He had a high-output circulatory state and a cardiomyopathy, which caused cardiac insufficiency 22 years before the skeletal myopathy presented. His venous lactate levels were elevated, and at one stage of the illness he developed severe lactic acidosis. Electron microscopy of his muscle showed various mitochondrial abnormalities and an accumulation of neutral lipids. Histochemistry and thin-layer chromatography confirmed the lipid accumulation.

paragraphs.text: Saunders et al. (2015) described a 7-year-old girl (CMH193) who was evaluated for suspected mitochondrial myopathy. She had no symptoms and met her developmental milestones in the first year, apart from toe-walking. She had a positive Gowers sign at age 2 years and had lost the ability to walk by age 3. Her disease progressed to include proximal muscle weakness, dysarthria, a decline in fine motor skills, dysmetria, and hypotonia that evolved into spasticity. She also developed dystonia and complex partial seizures, with left temporal lobe spikes on EEG. She had a very lean body habitus and did not gain weight, and her lactic acidosis required bicarbonate supplementation. Brain MRI at 33 months showed subtle increased signal in the medial globus pallidus on both sides. This was no longer seen 2 years later, which the authors suggested reflected maturation of myelination. MR spectroscopy and head CT were normal. A quadriceps muscle biopsy at age 4 showed variable fiber size, with isolated small atrophic fibers of all subtypes and no ragged red fibers. On electron microscopy, the mitochondria showed marked disarray of their cristae and globular dense osmiophilic inclusions. There were also subsarcolemmal aggregates of abnormal mitochondria with concentric lamellar membranes, suggesting degenerating mitochondria. Secondary lysosomes containing mitochondria-derived residual bodies were increased, but no pathogenic variants were found in lipofuscinosis genes.

paragraphs.text: Shukla et al. (2018) also described a girl (patient 2) of Indian/Fijian origin born to nonconsanguineous parents. She developed normally until about 13 months of age and then regressed, with episodes of epilepsia partialis continua and focal seizures that were difficult to control. She became nonverbal and required gastrostomy feeding. She had acquired microcephaly (49 cm, -4.7 SD at 15 years), central hypotonia with muscle weakness, choreiform movements, dystonia, proximal weakness, absent reflexes and severe contractures. Brain MRI showed progressive atrophy of the cerebellum, brainstem, and parietal and occipital lobes, with thinning of the corpus callosum, and MRS showed a persistently elevated lipid-lactate peak. Her muscle biopsy showed enlarged, irregularly shaped mitochondria with membrane whorls and disrupted cristae, with normal complex I-IV activities. She also had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with subaortic stenosis, elevated blood lactate, elevated GDF15, reduced visual evoked potentials and obstructive sleep apnea.

paragraphs.text: Burnyte et al. (2023) reported 2 adult sibs, a brother and a sister, with slowly progressive ataxia and sensorimotor polyneuropathy beginning at age 14 years. Their cognition stayed normal over time. At age 14 the brother developed weakness and distal atrophy of the lower limbs, with ataxia and a gait disturbance. By age 30 he had marked axial ataxia, tetraparesis, hypotonia, wasting of the calves and feet, absent lower-limb reflexes, foot deformities, bilateral Babinski signs, dysmetria and mild length-dependent hypoesthesia. Nerve conduction studies showed a sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy. He could no longer walk from age 44. At age 45 he had mild dysarthria and horizontal nystagmus. Brain MRI showed mild cerebellar atrophy, and his MMSE score was 30/30. His sister had difficulty walking and weakness of both lower limbs from age 14 years. At age 21 she had distal atrophy of the upper and lower limbs, absent lower-limb reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, severe axial ataxia and appendicular dysmetria, and she could not keep an upright posture. Her cranial nerve and cognitive examinations were normal. Nerve conduction studies showed an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy, and EMG showed no myopathic changes. Neither sib had cognitive decline or visual, auditory, cardiac or liver dysfunction. The disease advanced markedly in the teens but progressed only slightly through adulthood.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) reported 14 individuals (6 male, 8 female) with neurologic manifestations from 12 unrelated families with biallelic PNPLA8 variants. The families were of Japanese, Saudi Arabian, Iraqi, Afghan, Pakistani, Turkish, Lebanese, Egyptian, Iranian and Indian/Fijian origin. Ages at last assessment ranged from 3 days to 33 years. Common features were central hypotonia (13/13), dystonia (8/12), seizures (10/14) and cerebellar atrophy (12/12). A severe group of 8 patients (Families 1-8) had congenital microcephaly (5/7), global developmental delay with no milestones attained (7/7), peripheral spasticity (7/8) and seizures beginning within the first 7 months of life (8/8). In this group, neuroimaging showed a simplified gyral pattern (6/6), pontocerebellar hypoplasia (7/7) and severe progressive atrophy of the cerebral cortex (5/5). Four patients (Families 11-12) had a relatively mild phenotype. All 4 learned to walk and later lost milestones; 3 of 4 had ataxia, 3 of 4 had mild or no intellectual disability, and seizures were isolated or absent. Brain MRI in this group showed little or no loss of cerebral cortical volume but progressive cerebellar atrophy. Patients in Families 9 and 10 were of intermediate severity and also had cerebellar atrophy. Combining these patients with 11 previously reported individuals (25 individuals from 20 families), the authors concluded that PNPLA8-related neurologic disease is a continuum, from developmental and/or degenerative epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy to childhood-onset neurodegeneration.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) used exome or genome sequencing, with segregation analysis by Sanger sequencing, to study 14 patients from 12 families. They identified 14 PNPLA8 variants, 12 of them novel: 4 nonsense, 5 frameshift, 3 intronic variants near exon-intron boundaries and 2 missense variants. Each variant had a frequency below 0.001% in population databases including gnomAD. Twelve of the 14 individuals carried combinations of nonsense, frameshift and splice-site variants, suggesting loss of function. In Patient 1, a Japanese boy from a nonconsanguineous family in the severe group who died at age 4 years, the c.1625+3_1625+6del variant caused aberrant splicing with skipping of exons 6-8 in lymphoblastoid cells. His skin fibroblasts showed a significant reduction of the 77-kDa PNPLA8 protein, indicating a null effect. The frameshift mutation p.Glu296Lysfs*6 in Patient 6, also in the severe group, likewise had a null effect on PNPLA8 protein expression in skin fibroblasts. SpliceAI predicted loss of the splice acceptor site for the intronic variants c.2075-2A-G in Patient 2 (delta score 0.97) and c.1684-2A-G in Patient 5 (delta score 0.93), both in the severe group. Their effect on splicing was not tested experimentally. Fibroblasts from a patient homozygous for the previously reported missense mutation p.Val520Asp, who had a severe phenotype, showed protein expression similar to that of controls. The authors also identified 2 individuals from 2 unrelated Iranian families in a non-neurologic cohort who were homozygous for distinct N-terminal frameshift variants in PNPLA8 affecting only the largest (88-kDa) isoform. One had optic atrophy and the other had nonsyndromic hearing loss. An affected sib in the optic atrophy family was heterozygous, and the authors considered these variants of undetermined significance. Fibroblasts from Patient 14, who carried p.Val7*, showed weak expression of the 77-kDa protein.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) made PNPLA8 knockout cerebral organoids from CRISPR/Cas9-edited human iPSCs. At 12 weeks, the organoids had smaller subventricular zone-like regions, fewer PAX6+HOPX+ basal radial glial cells and fewer SATB2+ upper-layer neurons. Ventricular zone size, deep-layer neurons, intermediate progenitors, mitosis and apoptosis were unchanged, and increased BrdU labeling suggested an altered S-phase length in the ventricular zone. Organoids derived from iPSCs of Patient 1 reproduced the knockout phenotype compared with organoids from his father, confirming the loss-of-function nature of his variants. Spatial transcriptomics of the ventricular zone of the patient's organoids showed enrichment of gene sets for neuron differentiation, cell cycle and lysophospholipid pathways, with reduced basal radial glia gene signatures. The authors suggested that loss of PNPLA8 alters the fate specification of apical radial glial cells. Mitochondrial morphology and OXPHOS activity were essentially unaffected in PNPLA8 knockout neural progenitor cells (NPCs). The authors suggested that NPCs depend mainly on glycolysis, whereas mitochondrial dysfunction in OXPHOS-dependent neurons might contribute to progressive cerebral and cerebellar neurodegeneration. Knockout NPCs had lower amounts of lysophosphatidic acid, lysophosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidic acid, while cardiolipin was unaffected. Adding lysophosphatidic acid for 7 days increased the number of basal radial glial cells in organoids from Patient 1. The authors concluded that PNPLA8-dependent phospholipid synthesis is crucial for the abundance of basal radial glia, and that biallelic null variants cause microcephaly through this mechanism.

paragraphs.text: Mancuso et al. (2009) found that mice lacking calcium-independent phospholipase A2-gamma (iPLA2-gamma-null mice) had major changes in hippocampal phospholipid metabolism. Shotgun lipidomics showed a markedly raised hippocampal cardiolipin content, with a shift toward shorter-chain molecular species. The mice also had changes in choline and ethanolamine glycerophospholipids, including less plasmenylethanolamine, more oxidized phosphatidylethanolamine species and more ceramides. Electron microscopy of the hippocampus showed enlarged heteromorphic lamellar structures undergoing degeneration, together with ubiquitin-positive spheroid inclusion bodies. These structures were purified by buoyant density centrifugation and identified as degenerating mitochondria by SDS-PAGE and proteomics. The authors concluded that loss of iPLA2-gamma function causes a mitochondrial neurodegenerative disorder marked by degenerating mitochondria, autophagy and cognitive dysfunction.

paragraphs.text: In Patient 1, a Japanese boy from a nonconsanguineous family who belonged to the severe group and died at age 4 years, Nakamura et al.
